summary: The Wastewater calculator turns the average untreated influent BOD, the average untreated influent COD and more into effluent COD. Think of it as a shortcut for an animal, a plant or a biological process whose scale you want to put into perspective. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Wastewater calculator work?
sections.html:
The Wastewater calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports effluent COD in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the average untreated influent BOD, the average untreated influent COD, the average primary treated COD and the effluent SS concentration.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Wastewater calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Effluent COD=-average primary treated COD + average untreated influent COD
Average primary treated BOD=average untreated influent BOD − effluent BOD
Effluent COD=COD loading ÷ effluent flow
Effluent flow=BOD loading ÷ effluent BOD
Free-board=-volume ÷ (length × width) + side wall depth
Width=-volume ÷ (length × (free-board − side wall depth))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Wastewater calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Comparing two organisms, populations or processes
  • Supporting a lesson, a lecture or a field note
  • Putting a biological quantity into a scale you can picture
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the average untreated influent BOD, the average untreated influent COD and the average primary treated COD — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Wastewater calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns effluent COD, derived from the average untreated influent BOD, the average untreated influent COD and the average primary treated COD. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Wastewater calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the average untreated influent BOD, the average untreated influent COD, the average primary treated COD and the effluent SS concentration, which is 27 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter influent SS weight in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Influent SS weight opens in kilograms and the chip beside it offers 29 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (4 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Wastewater calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
